stories.title: Australia usually hosts the world's biggest cuttlefish mating event - not this year
stories.summary: Every winter, a sliver of the South Australian coast hosts the world's largest mating event for giant cuttlefish. Some years, hundreds of thousands of the unique marine species endemic to Australia gather along the Cuttlefish Coast for the annual mating season, bringing their colourful, shape-shifting figures to the shallow waters and attracting thousands of keen divers. But this year, the turnout was the lowest on record, sparking concerns of a "catastrophic decline" of the species. Official figures released this month estimate just 1,811 cuttlefish turned up to mate this year, down from 63,000 last year - a 97% drop. The state government says a toxic algal bloom that has ravaged the state's coastline for more than 18 months may be to blame for the sharp decline. The low figures have also prompted calls for the species to be listed as endangered. Adult cuttlefish typically die after breeding so each mating season is crucial for the species' future, but in recent months, just 440 eggs have been counted, instead of the millions that are usually laid. Manny Katz, 28, was one of four divers who spent hours along the coast last month to observe the annual breeding event, having been tasked by South Australia's Department of Environment and Water (DEW). "Because there have been so few cuttlefish, DEW thought it would be worth going out and trying to do an assessment of how many eggs there currently are around the coastline to understand what the population is going to be next year." Over two days in July, his team did eight one-hour dives, exploring the undersides of rocky reefs to count the eggs. "Along the eight kilometres (five miles) of coastline, there would normally be millions of eggs," he said, as each female can lay dozens of egg and tens of thousands usually turn up to breed. "[We] pretty much looked under every single rock that we could have and we only found about 440 eggs."
